correctness.rationale: The published prerequisites are the minimum-distance necessity for binary k-PIR codes and the exact optimum \(P(4,4)=9\). The verifier exhausts all \(817190\) multisets of nine nonzero columns, identifies exactly \(1345\) with minimum distance at least \(4\), checks every nonzero target by two independent exact four-set-packing predicates, and obtains exactly \(1120\) basis-flexible four-PIR multisets. Full enumeration of \(\operatorname{GL}(4,2)\) gives orbit sizes \(280,840\) and stabilizers \(72,24\). Zero columns are excluded rigorously because deleting one preserves every nonzero recovery equation and would contradict \(P(4,4)=9\).

originality.rationale: Foundational, optimal-systematic-construction, and short-block full texts were compared at statement level. They define the same recovery-set object, provide a projective optimal construction, and prove the length-nine optimum, but do not state the exhaustive two-orbit equality classification, the \(1120=280+840\) census, or the recovery-profile dichotomy. Exact-parameter and equivalence searches produced no covering result. Residual risk is an obscure unindexed census.
residual_risks: An obscure or unindexed finite census of the same optimizer set may exist.

Ordinary binary linear-code databases may classify some underlying \([9,4,4]\) codes, but no inspected source was found that combines such data with the PIR information-basis predicate to imply the two-orbit claim.

value.rationale: The result determines the entire equality layer at a natural storage-optimal PIR parameter, not a selected subfamily. It shows that the well-motivated projective construction is only one of exactly two optimizer types, identifies a genuinely nonprojective optimum, and supplies a sharp recovery-profile invariant (all \(15\) versus exactly \(14\) nonzero targets). This is a reusable finite benchmark for constructions and equivalence testing.
